title: Search Engine Discovery and Reconnaissance
objective: Identify what sensitive design and configuration information of the application, system, or organization is exposed directly or indirectly through search engines.
description: Search engines index web content and may expose sensitive information that should not be publicly accessible. This test identifies indexed pages containing sensitive data, configuration files, test environments, and other information that could aid an attacker.
prerequisites: Access to popular search engines. Knowledge of advanced search operators (dorking). Understanding of the application structure and potential sensitive content.
testing_steps:
1. Use search engines to query the target domain using site: operator.
2. Apply advanced search operators to find specific file types (ext:pdf, ext:sql, ext:bak).
3. Search for common sensitive paths (admin, backup, test, staging).
4. Check cached versions of pages for removed content.
5. Use Google Hacking Database (GHDB) queries relevant to the technology stack.
6. Repeat across multiple search engines (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo).
expected_result: Identification of exposed sensitive information through search engines. Documentation of indexed pages that should not be publicly accessible.
required_evidence: Screenshots of search results showing sensitive content. List of discovered URLs with sensitive information. Cache snapshots showing removed but still indexed content.
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-INFO-01. Google Hacking Database (GHDB). Exploit-DB GHDB section.

title: Web Server Fingerprinting
objective: Identify the type and version of the web server and its components to understand potential vulnerabilities associated with that version.
description: Web servers often reveal their identity through HTTP response headers, error pages, and default configurations. Fingerprinting helps identify the server type and version, which can then be cross-referenced with known vulnerabilities.
prerequisites: Access to the target application. Understanding of HTTP protocol and response headers. Knowledge of common web server characteristics.
testing_steps:
1. Send HTTP requests and analyze response headers (Server, X-Powered-By, X-AspNet-Version).
2. Request non-existent pages to trigger default error pages and analyze their format.
3. Test different HTTP methods (OPTIONS, TRACE) to observe server behavior.
4. Request pages with different extensions to observe response differences.
5. Use automated fingerprinting tools (httprint, WhatWeb, Wappalyzer).
6. Analyze cookie names for framework identification (e.g., ASP.NET_SessionId, PHPSESSID).
7. Check for default installation files and directories.
expected_result: Identification of the web server type, version, and supporting technologies. Documentation of the technology stack including server software, framework versions, and additional components.
required_evidence: Screenshots of identified headers and error pages. Tool output showing server and technology identification. List of identified technologies with version numbers.
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-INFO-02. Netcraft: https://www.netcraft.com. WhatWeb: https://github.com/urbanadventurer/WhatWeb.

title: Testing for Authentication Bypass
objective: Identify vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to bypass the authentication mechanism and gain unauthorized access to the application.
description: Authentication bypass vulnerabilities occur when flaws in the authentication logic allow an attacker to access protected resources without valid credentials. Common techniques include parameter modification, SQL injection in login forms, and exploiting misconfigured access controls.
prerequisites: Understanding of the application's authentication mechanism. Access to a test account (or ability to create one). Knowledge of common authentication bypass techniques.
testing_steps:
1. Attempt to access protected pages directly without authentication.
2. Test parameter modification - change role, admin, authenticated parameters.
3. Try SQL injection in username/password fields (e.g., ' OR 1=1 --).
4. Test for NoSQL injection in login forms.
5. Check for hardcoded backdoor credentials in source code.
6. Attempt to use remember-me tokens without valid session.
7. Test for type juggling vulnerabilities in authentication logic.
8. Attempt path traversal in authentication redirects.
expected_result: Identification of any authentication bypass vulnerabilities. Successful reconstruction of bypass methods for verified vulnerabilities.
required_evidence: HTTP request/response pairs showing the bypass. Screenshots of accessing protected areas without authentication. Proof-of-concept demonstrating the bypass.
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-AUTHN-04. OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet. CWE-287: Improper Authentication.

title: Testing for Reflected Cross-Site Scripting
objective: Identify reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities where an attacker can inject client-side scripts into web pages viewed by other users.
description: Reflected XSS occurs when user input is immediately returned by a web application in an error message, search result, or any other response that includes the input data as part of the request without proper sanitization. This allows attackers to craft malicious URLs that execute scripts in victims' browsers.
prerequisites: Understanding of HTML, JavaScript, and XSS attack vectors. Access to the application with various input parameters. Knowledge of browser security mechanisms and XSS filters.
testing_steps: 1. Identify all user-controllable input parameters (GET, POST, headers, cookies). 2. For each parameter, inject basic XSS probes: , . 3. Test different HTML contexts: tag body, attribute values, JavaScript strings, CSS values. 4. Test with encoded payloads: URL encoding, HTML entity encoding, Unicode escapes. 5. Bypass common filters using case variations and alternative syntax. 6. Test DOM-based XSS by analyzing JavaScript that processes URL fragments. 7. Verify the payload actually executes in the browser. 8. Document the exact injection point and payload for each finding.
expected_result: Identification of all reflected XSS vulnerabilities with working proof-of-concept payloads. Classification of each finding by context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript).
required_evidence: Working PoC URL that triggers the XSS when visited. Screenshots of the alert/script execution. The exact unfiltered input parameter and payload. HTTP request/response pair showing the reflected input.
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-INPV-01. OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet. PortSwigger XSS Cheat Sheet. CWE-79: Cross-Site Scripting.

title: Testing for SQL Injection
objective: Identify SQL injection vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to interfere with the queries an application makes to its database.
description: SQL injection occurs when user-supplied data is incorporated into SQL queries without proper sanitization. This can allow attackers to view, modify, or delete data, and in some cases execute commands on the underlying operating system. SQL injection remains one of the most critical web application vulnerabilities.
prerequisites: Understanding of SQL syntax for target database systems. Access to the application with input parameters. Knowledge of SQL injection detection and exploitation techniques.
testing_steps:
1. Identify all input vectors that may interact with a database.
2. For each vector, test with single quote (') to trigger syntax errors.
3. Use boolean-based detection: ' OR 1=1 -- vs ' OR 1=2 -- to confirm injection.
4. Use time-based detection: '; WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:05'-- for blind SQLi.
5. Determine the number of columns using ORDER BY or UNION SELECT NULL.
6. Extract database version and table names using UNION-based injection.
7. Test for stacked queries (multiple statements in one request).
8. Use automated tools (sqlmap) for comprehensive testing.
9. Test for second-order SQLi where input is stored then later used in queries.
10. Ensure all testing is authorized and within scope.
expected_result: Identification of all SQL injection vulnerabilities. Database version and structure information (if safely extractable). Working PoC demonstrating data extraction capability.
required_evidence: HTTP requests demonstrating the injection. Screenshots of error messages or extracted data. sqlmap or equivalent tool output. Proof-of-concept showing database access.
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-INPV-05. OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet. CWE-89: SQL Injection. sqlmap: https://sqlmap.org.

title: Testing Session Management
objective: Evaluate the security of session management mechanisms to ensure session tokens cannot be predicted, stolen, or manipulated.
description: Session management is a critical security component. Weak session token generation, improper session invalidation, and session fixation vulnerabilities can allow attackers to hijack user sessions and impersonate legitimate users.
prerequisites: Understanding of session management concepts and HTTP state mechanisms. Access to authenticated sessions. Knowledge of session security best practices.
testing_steps:
1. Collect multiple session tokens and analyze their randomness and entropy.
2. Test for session fixation: set a known session ID before authentication and check if it persists after login.
3. Test session token reuse after logout.
4. Check if session tokens are transmitted over HTTPS only.
5. Verify session tokens are invalidated server-side on logout.
6. Test concurrent session handling (multiple simultaneous logins).
7. Check for session token leakage in URLs, Referer headers, or logs.
8. Test session timeout (idle and absolute).
9. Verify cookie attributes: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path.
expected_result: Analysis of session token entropy and predictability. Identification of session fixation and hijacking vulnerabilities. Documentation of any session management weaknesses.
required_evidence: Multiple session tokens for entropy analysis. HTTP traffic showing session token handling. Screenshots of session-related cookie attributes. Evidence of session persistence after logout (if applicable).
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-SESS-01 through SESS-06. OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet. CWE-384: Session Fixation.

title: Testing Business Logic
objective: Identify flaws in the business logic that could allow an attacker to circumvent business rules and processes in ways not intended by the application designers.
description: Business logic vulnerabilities are unique to each application and arise from flaws in the design and implementation of business rules. These cannot be detected by automated scanners and require human understanding of the application's intended behavior.
prerequisites: Deep understanding of the application's business processes and workflows. Test accounts with different privilege levels. Knowledge of common business logic attack patterns.
testing_steps:
1. Thoroughly map all business workflows and state transitions.
2. For each workflow, attempt to skip steps by directly accessing later URLs.
3. Test negative values in quantity, price, and numeric fields.
4. Test for integer overflow in numeric business calculations.
5. Attempt to exceed business limits (quantity, frequency, value).
6. Test race conditions by sending concurrent requests.
7. Verify all server-side validations match client-side restrictions.
8. Test time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) scenarios.
9. Attempt to exploit order of operations in multi-step processes.
10. Check if business rules can be bypassed via API calls directly.
expected_result: Documentation of all business logic vulnerabilities. Working proof-of-concept for each identified flaw. Business impact analysis for each vulnerability.
required_evidence: Request/response sequences showing workflow bypass. Screenshots of unexpected application behavior. Evidence of business rule circumvention. Impact demonstration (e.g., negative balance, unauthorized discount).
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-BUSL-01 through BUSL-08. OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) V4.0. CWE-840: Business Logic Errors.

title: Testing for Weak Transport Layer Security
objective: Evaluate the TLS/SSL implementation to ensure that communications between the client and server are properly encrypted and not susceptible to protocol-level attacks.
description: Transport Layer Security is critical for protecting data in transit. Weak TLS configurations can expose communications to eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks, and protocol downgrade attacks. This test verifies the TLS version, cipher suites, certificate validity, and configuration.
prerequisites: Network access to the target server. Understanding of TLS/SSL protocols and common vulnerabilities. Knowledge of cipher suite strength and cryptographic best practices.
testing_steps:
1. Verify that HTTPS is enforced and HTTP is redirected to HTTPS.
2. Check supported TLS versions - disable SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1.
3. Verify TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 are enabled and preferred.
4. Analyze cipher suite configuration for weak ciphers (RC4, DES, 3DES, EXPORT, NULL).
5. Check for Forward Secrecy support (ECDHE/DHE key exchange).
6. Verify the certificate chain: valid issuer, not expired, correct hostname.
7. Test for insecure renegotiation vulnerability.
8. Check for compression-related attacks (CRIME, BREACH).
9. Verify HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) header configuration.
10. Test for certificate pinning implementation.
expected_result: Comprehensive TLS configuration report. Identification of weak protocol versions and cipher suites. Certificate chain analysis results. Specific remediation recommendations.
required_evidence: SSL Labs or testssl.sh scan output. Screenshots of weak TLS configurations. Certificate details including issuer, validity period, and chain. HSTS header verification results.
references: OWASP Testing Guide v4.2: WSTG-CRYP-01. OWASP Transport Layer Protection Cheat Sheet. SSL Labs: https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/. Mozilla TLS Configuration Guide.
